hint1: You will find lots of these in a school science lab.
hint2: It is tall and thin, with lines and numbers up the side.
hint3: Drop a stone in and the water level goes up.
hint4: Read it at eye level to find how many cm³ of water are in it.

hint1: Every quantity in physics is either this type or the other type.
hint2: Mass, energy, time and temperature are all examples.
hint3: Speed is one, but velocity is not.
hint4: It tells you how much, but never which way.

hint1: Two of these at right angles can be added using Pythagoras.
hint2: Force, velocity, acceleration and momentum are all examples.
hint3: Weight is one, but mass is not.
hint4: It has a size and also tells you which way.

hint1: Every road has a limit for it.
hint2: In physics, we give it in m/s.
hint3: Usain Bolt's was about 10 m/s in the 100 m race.
hint4: Divide the distance by the time to find it.

hint1: It can be positive or negative.
hint2: '5 m/s to the left' is one.
hint3: A car going round a bend at a steady 20 km/h keeps changing it.
hint4: How quickly something moves, and which way.

hint1: Runners in a race all cover the same one.
hint2: A marathon's is about 42 km.
hint3: Speed × time gives you this.
hint4: How many metres or kilometres it is from A to B.

hint1: Sports car adverts love it: 0 to 100 km/h in a few seconds.
hint2: A sprinter has lots of it just after the starting gun.
hint3: Its unit is m/s², not m/s.
hint4: A falling object's is about 9.8 m/s² near the Earth.

hint1: A plane landing on a short runway needs a lot of it.
hint2: On a speed–time graph, the line slopes down.
hint3: Its unit is m/s², the same as its opposite.
hint4: A car stopping suddenly at a red light has a big one.

hint1: In a fair test, you keep most things like this.
hint2: Melting ice stays at 0 °C: its temperature is this.
hint3: A straight, sloping line on a distance–time graph shows this kind of speed.
hint4: 'The car travels at a ___ speed of 20 m/s.'

hint1: A sleeping cat on the sofa is this.
hint2: Its speed is 0 m/s.
hint3: On a distance–time graph, a flat line shows this.
hint4: A parked car is this.

hint1: Maths and physics teachers both ask you to work it out from a graph.
hint2: A flat road has none; a mountain road has a big one.
hint3: Divide the change up by the change across.
hint4: On a distance–time graph, it tells you the speed.

hint1: Raindrops reach it long before they hit the ground.
hint2: The resultant force is zero, but the object is still moving down.
hint3: The steady top speed of something dropping through the sky.
hint4: Opening a parachute gives you a new, much lower one.

hint1: Everything has some, even air.
hint2: We find it with a balance in the lab.
hint3: It stays the same on the Moon as on Earth.
hint4: We measure it in kg, not in newtons.

hint1: Astronauts have less of it on the Moon.
hint2: It always acts straight down, towards the centre of the Earth.
hint3: It is a force, so we measure it in newtons.
hint4: On Earth, a 1 kg bag has about 10 N of it.

hint1: It is different on the Moon, on Mars and on Jupiter.
hint2: Jupiter's is about two and a half times the Earth's.
hint3: It tells you how many newtons act on each kilogram.
hint4: On Earth it is about 9.8 N/kg.

hint1: It explains why a stone sinks but a log does not.
hint2: Gold has much more of it than water.
hint3: Water's is about 1 g/cm³.
hint4: How much stuff is packed into each cm³.

hint1: Every box, bottle and stone has it.
hint2: We give it in cm³ or m³.
hint3: Drop a stone into water and the water goes up by this much.
hint4: Length × width × height of a box.

hint1: A rubber duck does this in the bath.
hint2: Wood does this, but a stone does not.
hint3: Ice does this in a glass of cola.
hint4: A big steel ship does this and does not go down.

hint1: Gravity is one; a magnet makes one too.
hint2: It can make a ball start, stop or change shape.
hint3: In diagrams, we draw it as an arrow.
hint4: You need one to kick a ball or open a door.

hint1: In a tug of war, it decides which way the rope moves.
hint2: If it is zero, an object stays still or keeps moving at a steady speed.
hint3: 10 N left plus 4 N right gives 6 N left.
hint4: One push or pull with the same effect as all of them together.

hint1: Without it, your feet would slip and you could not walk.
hint2: It makes a bike's brakes work.
hint3: It is low on ice and high on sandpaper.
hint4: The force between a tyre and the road.

hint1: Cyclists bend down low to get less of it.
hint2: Sports cars have smooth shapes to cut it.
hint3: The faster a car goes, the more of it there is.
hint4: It pushes up on a falling skydiver and slows them down.

hint1: Hooke's law is all about this.
hint2: Hang more masses on a rubber band and this gets bigger.
hint3: Measure with a ruler before and after adding a load, then subtract.
hint4: A bungee rope grows from 10 m to 25 m: this is 15 m.

hint1: A steel wire or a metal coil reaches it if you load it enough.
hint2: Past this point, the load–stretch graph begins to curve.
hint3: Beyond it, doubling the load no longer doubles the stretch.
hint4: The point where a metal coil stops obeying F = kx.

hint1: It can be clockwise or anticlockwise.
hint2: Its unit is the newton metre (N m).
hint3: A longer spanner gives a bigger one for the same push.
hint4: Everyday meaning: a very short time, as in 'Wait a ___!'

hint1: Scissors have one where the two blades cross.
hint2: Your elbow works as one for your lower arm.
hint3: A door swings around one at its side.
hint4: Two children go up and down around it in the playground.

hint1: A tightrope walker tries hard to stay in it.
hint2: A book lying on a table is in this state.
hint3: Clockwise moments equal anticlockwise moments.
hint4: No overall force and no overall turning effect act on it.

hint1: Hang a card shape from a pin, and a plumb line helps you find it.
hint2: For a 30 cm ruler, it is at the 15 cm mark.
hint3: If it ends up outside the base, the object falls over.
hint4: A bus with a low one is hard to tip over.

hint1: Engineers want every building and bridge to be this.
hint2: Racing cars are built low and wide to be this.
hint3: A wide base makes a lamp more like this.
hint4: Hard to knock over, like a pyramid.

hint1: In a crash, the total before equals the total after.
hint2: Its unit is kg m/s.
hint3: A heavy lorry has lots of it, even when moving slowly.
hint4: 'The team has ___ after three wins in a row.'

hint1: A footballer's kick gives the ball one, and off it flies.
hint2: Its unit is N s, which is the same as kg m/s.
hint3: For the object it acts on, it equals mv − mu.
hint4: Newtons × seconds: how hard and for how long you push.

hint1: Scientists at CERN study these between tiny particles.
hint2: Snooker balls have them all the time.
hint3: Total momentum is the same before and after one.
hint4: Two bumper cars banging into each other make one.

hint1: The Sun sends it to Earth every day.
hint2: Moving cars, hot kettles and stretched springs all have it.
hint3: A tired person feels they have very little.
hint4: Breakfast gives you this, so you can run and play.

hint1: A rolling bowling ball has lots of it.
hint2: A parked car has none.
hint3: Go twice as fast and you have four times as much.
hint4: The store of anything that is not still.

hint1: Water held behind a dam stores lots of it.
hint2: A rollercoaster has the most at the top of the first hill.
hint3: A book on a top shelf has more than one on the floor.
hint4: Climbing the stairs gives your body more of this store.

hint1: Plants turn sunlight into it.
hint2: Coal and wood give it out when they burn.
hint3: A chocolate bar is full of it.
hint4: Calories on a snack packet tell you how much there is.

hint1: A trampoline holds it when you land on it.
hint2: An archer's bow is full of it just before the arrow flies.
hint3: A pulled-back catapult has lots of it.
hint4: The store in anything bent or pulled out of shape that wants to go back.

hint1: Every object has some, even an ice cube.
hint2: A kettle of water gains it as it warms up.
hint3: A warm bath has more than a cup of boiling water.
hint4: The kinetic plus potential stores of all the atoms inside something.

hint1: Scientists have never found anything that breaks this rule.
hint2: A dropped ball never bounces back higher than where it started.
hint3: On a Sankey diagram, the arrows out add up to the arrow in.
hint4: The rule that joules are never made or lost, only moved between stores.

hint1: Pushing a heavy box across the floor needs lots of it.
hint2: Pushing hard on a wall that never moves gives none.
hint3: Lifting a box higher needs more of it.
hint4: Multiply the newtons by the metres moved.

hint1: Every kettle and hair dryer has a number for it on the label.
hint2: A kettle with a higher one boils water faster.
hint3: It tells you how many joules are moved every second.
hint4: When the lights go off in a storm, we call it a ___ cut.

hint1: Engineers always try to improve it in engines and lamps.
hint2: It can never be more than 100 out of 100.
hint3: An LED lamp has a higher one than a filament lamp.
hint4: Joules you want out ÷ joules you put in.

hint1: Many countries want more of their electricity from this kind of source.
hint2: Waves, tides and hot rocks underground give this kind of energy.
hint3: The Three Gorges Dam makes this kind of electricity.
hint4: Nature makes it again, so we never use it all up.

hint1: Most of the world's electricity still comes from this kind of source.
hint2: Natural gas and uranium are this kind of resource.
hint3: Once we use it, nature cannot make more in our lifetime.
hint4: Unlike solar or wind, one day there will be none left.

hint1: Many power stations still use it.
hint2: Using it puts carbon dioxide into the air.
hint3: It formed from plants and animals that died millions of years ago.
hint4: Petrol and diesel are made from one.

hint1: It happens inside the reactors at Daya Bay power station.
hint2: Each one releases neutrons that can trigger the next: a chain reaction.
hint3: A slow neutron is taken in first, and then lots of energy comes out.
hint4: Like fusion in reverse: one heavy centre breaks into two lighter ones.

hint1: Scientists hope it will give the world clean energy one day.
hint2: China's EAST machine in Hefei tests this process.
hint3: Two tiny centres of atoms crash together to make one bigger centre.
hint4: It powers the stars, including the one closest to us.

hint1: Divers feel more of it the deeper they go.
hint2: Pump up a bike tyre and it rises inside.
hint3: A sharp knife cuts well because it gives a high one.
hint4: Before big tests, students feel exam ___.

hint1: Everything around you is made of them.
hint2: You cannot see one, even with a school microscope.
hint3: In a gas, they fly around fast in all directions.
hint4: A very, very little bit of stuff.

hint1: Radioactive decay is like this: nobody can say which nucleus goes next.
hint2: A lottery picks its numbers this way.
hint3: 'Gas particles move in ___ directions.'
hint4: Every roll of a dice gives this kind of number.

hint1: Scientists have got very close to it, but never reached it.
hint2: Deep space is chilly, but still warmer than this.
hint3: Here, particles have the least possible kinetic energy.
hint4: It is about −273 °C.

hint1: Chocolate does this in a hot car.
hint2: Snowmen do it in the sun.
hint3: Pure water does this at 0 °C.
hint4: The opposite of freezing.

hint1: Cooking pasta starts with this.
hint2: On top of Mount Everest, water does it at a lower temperature.
hint3: It happens all through the water, not only at the top.
hint4: Pure water does it at 100 °C.

hint1: It is part of the water cycle.
hint2: Wet clothes on a washing line lose their water this way.
hint3: Sweat cools your skin through this.
hint4: Unlike boiling, it happens only at the surface, at any temperature.

hint1: It is the step in the water cycle where clouds form.
hint2: The bathroom mirror goes misty after a shower because of this.
hint3: Drops appear on the outside of a chilled can of cola.
hint4: The opposite of evaporation.

hint1: Lava turns into rock this way.
hint2: Melted chocolate in a mould turns firm by this.
hint3: Water does it at 0 °C as it cools down.
hint4: The opposite of melting.

hint1: The Eiffel Tower is several centimetres taller in summer because of it.
hint2: Railway lines have small gaps to allow for it.
hint3: A liquid-in-glass thermometer works because of it.
hint4: Most materials grow a little when their temperature rises.

hint1: The sea warms up more slowly than the beach because of it.
hint2: Copper has a low one, so a copper pan gets hot quickly.
hint3: In ΔE = mcΔθ, it is the letter c.
hint4: The joules needed to warm 1000 g of a substance by 1 °C.

hint1: One of three ways thermal energy travels.
hint2: It works well in copper but badly in plastic and air.
hint3: Particles shake and pass energy on to the ones next to them.
hint4: Why a spoon left in soup soon burns your fingers.

hint1: It happens in a pan of soup on the cooker.
hint2: Warm water goes up, cool water sinks, round and round.
hint3: It can't happen in a solid, because the particles can't move from place to place.
hint4: Why the top bunk bed is warmer than the bottom one.

hint1: You feel it on your face as you sit by a campfire.
hint2: Dull black surfaces give out and take in the most.
hint3: Unlike conduction and convection, it needs no particles at all.
hint4: How energy from our nearest star crosses empty space to reach us.

hint1: Saucepans are made from a good one, so food cooks quickly.
hint2: Gold, silver and graphite are all good ones.
hint3: Charge or thermal energy passes through it easily.
hint4: The wire inside a cable is one; its plastic coat is not.

hint1: Saucepan handles are made of one.
hint2: Wool, air and foam are all good ones.
hint3: Thermal energy and charge can hardly pass through it.
hint4: It covers the copper inside a phone charger cable.

hint1: Convection can only happen in one.
hint2: Air, honey and water are all examples, but ice is not.
hint3: Its particles can slide past each other, so it has no fixed shape.
hint4: 'Drink plenty of ___s,' the doctor says when you have a cold.

hint1: Water ripples on a pond are this type.
hint2: A Mexican wave in a football stadium is a good model of it.
hint3: All electromagnetic waves, from radio to gamma, are like this.
hint4: The vibrations are at 90° to the way the wave travels.

hint1: Some earthquake waves are this type.
hint2: Push and pull a slinky along its length to make one.
hint3: It has squashed parts and stretched-out parts.
hint4: The vibrations go back and forth along the way the wave travels.

hint1: Storm waves at sea have a big one.
hint2: On a wave diagram, you measure it up and down, not along.
hint3: Turn up the volume and this gets bigger.
hint4: The distance from the middle line to the top of a crest.

hint1: Radio has a huge one; light has a tiny one.
hint2: Red light has a bigger one than blue light.
hint3: Its symbol is the Greek letter λ (lambda).
hint4: The gap from one top to the next top of a ripple.

hint1: Each radio station has its own, like 101.1 FM.
hint2: A dog whistle's is too high for people to hear.
hint3: A higher note on a piano has a higher one.
hint4: The number of waves passing a point each second.

hint1: White foam often forms here on sea waves.
hint2: A floating duck goes up to it, then down again.
hint3: Wavelength can be measured from one to the next.
hint4: The opposite of a trough on a wave.

hint1: A small boat sinks into one between two big waves.
hint2: The amplitude can be measured from the middle line to here.
hint3: As far under the middle line as a crest is over it.
hint4: The opposite of a crest.

hint1: You hear voices round a corner because of it.
hint2: It is greatest when the opening is about the size of the wavelength.
hint3: Long radio waves reach valleys behind hills because of it.
hint4: Water waves fan out after passing through a harbour entrance.

hint1: Trees look upside down in a still lake because of it.
hint2: An echo is the sound version of it.
hint3: A ball hitting a wall and coming straight back is a good model.
hint4: It lets you see your own face in a shop window.

hint1: It makes a swimming pool look shallower than it really is.
hint2: A pencil in water looks broken at the surface.
hint3: Contact lenses work because of it.
hint4: Light slows down going from air into water and changes its path.

hint1: Angles in ray diagrams are measured from it.
hint2: A ray travelling along it does not change course.
hint3: It stands at 90° to a mirror or the side of a glass block.
hint4: In daily life, the word means usual or ordinary.

hint1: Its symbol on diagrams is usually i.
hint2: Use a protractor, measuring from the dashed line, not the mirror.
hint3: When light hits a block head-on, this is zero.
hint4: The 'in' one; on a mirror it equals the 'out' one.

hint1: Diamonds sparkle partly because of it.
hint2: Doctors use it in endoscopes to look at a patient's stomach.
hint3: Above a certain angle, light cannot escape from water into air.
hint4: It traps light in the thin strands of internet cables.

hint1: Water's is about 49°; diamond's is about 24°.
hint2: At exactly this value, light skims along the surface.
hint3: Light in an optical fibre must hit the side above this.
hint4: Go past it, and no light escapes: it all stays trapped.

hint1: Cameras and human eyes both contain one.
hint2: Long-sighted people wear glasses with this kind.
hint3: It is fatter in the centre than at the edges.
hint4: Hold it in sunshine and it can burn a spot on paper.

hint1: Camera makers give it in millimetres, for example 50 mm.
hint2: A fatter, more curved piece of glass gives a shorter one.
hint3: Hold a magnifying glass in sunlight: it is how far away the bright spot is.
hint4: From the middle of the glass to the point where parallel rays meet.

hint1: It happens because each colour travels at a slightly different speed in glass.
hint2: Violet light bends the most and red light the least.
hint3: Sunlight passing through raindrops shows it as an arc of colours.
hint4: White light fanning out into its separate colours.

hint1: You can feel it in your throat when you hum.
hint2: Pluck a guitar string and you can see it.
hint3: On silent mode, your phone uses this to tell you about a call.
hint4: A very fast, tiny movement from side to side, again and again.

hint1: You might hear one in a big, empty room or a cave.
hint2: Ships use them to measure how deep the sea is.
hint3: Shout 'hello' in the mountains and hear 'hello... hello...'.
hint4: Hearing your own voice again from a far wall, a moment later.

hint1: Singers and violin players must get it exactly right.
hint2: A mouse's squeak and a lion's roar are very different in this.
hint3: A short, thin guitar string gives a squeaky one.
hint4: Not how loud a note is, but how squeaky or deep.

hint1: Doctors use it to look inside the body without X-rays.
hint2: Bats send it out to find insects in the dark.
hint3: Waves above 20 000 Hz, beyond what human ears can pick up.
hint4: Pregnant women see their unborn child on a screen thanks to it.

hint1: Iron filings crowd thickly around these.
hint2: The pull is strongest at these places.
hint3: Two of the same kind push apart; two different kinds pull together.
hint4: One is marked N, and the other is marked S.

hint1: You can't see it, but one surrounds the whole Earth.
hint2: Iron filings on paper show its shape as curved patterns.
hint3: The space round N and S poles where iron objects feel a pull.
hint4: Its arrows go out of the north pole and into the south pole.

hint1: Flowers do this to bees.
hint2: A rubbed balloon does this to small bits of paper.
hint3: The opposite of push away.
hint4: 'North and south poles ___ each other.'

hint1: Mosquito spray does this to insects.
hint2: Two balloons rubbed on your hair do this to each other.
hint3: Two north poles do this, so they will not touch.
hint4: The opposite of pull together.

hint1: Its unit is the coulomb (C).
hint2: Rub a balloon on your hair and it picks some up.
hint3: Two of the same kind push apart; opposite kinds pull together.
hint4: Current is the flow of this around a circuit.

hint1: It is far, far lighter than a proton.
hint2: In a metal wire, these move freely and carry the current.
hint3: It moves around the outside of every atom.
hint4: Beta radiation is a stream of speedy ones.

hint1: A big one through your body is very dangerous.
hint2: Its unit has the symbol A.
hint3: Use an ammeter to measure it.
hint4: Charge moving along a wire.

hint1: Mains sockets in China give 220 of its units.
hint2: Its meter is always connected in parallel.
hint3: A bigger value pushes a bigger current through the same lamp.
hint4: Current flows through a lamp; this is measured across it.

hint1: Like potential difference, it is measured in volts.
hint2: A bicycle dynamo produces this when its magnet spins.
hint3: The work a source does moving each coulomb round a complete circuit.
hint4: The '1.5 V' printed on the side of an AA cell.

hint1: A long, thin wire has more of it than a short, thick one.
hint2: Its unit symbol is Ω.
hint3: Work it out with R = V ÷ I.
hint4: How hard it is for charge to get through a component.

hint1: A lab meter with a needle or a digital screen.
hint2: Its circuit symbol is a circle with A inside.
hint3: Connect it in line with a lamp, never in parallel.
hint4: Like a voltmeter, but it shows the flow of charge.

hint1: A lab meter, often with a pointer or a digital display.
hint2: Its circuit symbol is a circle with V inside.
hint3: It goes across a component, never in line with it.
hint4: Use it to check whether a 1.5 V cell is still good.

hint1: A way of joining lamps in a circuit.
hint2: The current is the same at every point.
hint3: Old Christmas lights: if one bulb breaks, they all go dark.
hint4: Components joined one after another, with no branches.

hint1: The lights in your home are wired this way.
hint2: Voltmeters are always connected like this.
hint3: If one lamp breaks, the others stay on.
hint4: Each lamp has its own path back to the battery.

hint1: Each one has its own symbol in a diagram.
hint2: Engineers fix them onto a small board inside a phone.
hint3: Resistors, diodes and fuses are all examples.
hint4: One single piece of an electrical loop, like a bulb or a buzzer.

hint1: Digital thermometers often have one inside.
hint2: Fire alarms and car engines use one as a sensor.
hint3: As it warms up, current passes through it more easily.
hint4: Like an LDR, but it reacts to warmth instead of light.

hint1: Its symbol is a rectangle with two arrows pointing at it.
hint2: Garden lamps that switch on at sunset use one.
hint3: In sunshine current passes easily; at night it hardly passes at all.
hint4: Like a thermistor, but it reacts to sunshine instead of warmth.

hint1: Its symbol is a triangle pointing at a short line.
hint2: Phone chargers use them to turn AC into DC.
hint3: A special kind gives out light in traffic lights and torches.
hint4: Like a door that opens only forwards, never back.

hint1: Common sizes are 3 A, 5 A and 13 A.
hint2: It protects a kettle if too much current flows.
hint3: A thin strip inside gets very hot and breaks the circuit.
hint4: Unlike a circuit breaker, you replace it once it blows.

hint1: Plugs on metal kettles have one; many plastic hair dryers don't.
hint2: It is joined to the metal case of a toaster.
hint3: If a live part touches the metal case, it carries the current away.
hint4: Together with a fuse, it stops a faulty kettle giving you a shock.

hint1: Homes have a row of them in a box on the wall.
hint2: When there is a fault, it cuts off the current very quickly.
hint3: An electromagnet inside pulls a contact open when the current is too big.
hint4: When it clicks off, just push it back on: nothing to replace.

hint1: Michael Faraday discovered it in 1831.
hint2: Wireless phone chargers depend on it.
hint3: Push a magnet into a loop of wire and a meter needle flicks.
hint4: Making an e.m.f. by moving a wire through a magnetic field.

hint1: Power stations send this kind to homes and schools.
hint2: Transformers only work with this kind.
hint3: In China its frequency is 50 Hz.
hint4: The charge moves forwards, then backwards, again and again.

hint1: Solar panels produce this kind.
hint2: A phone charger changes mains into this for the phone.
hint3: On a graph against time, it is a flat line, not a wave.
hint4: What a torch cell gives: charge always flows the same way.

hint1: Grey boxes on poles near houses often hold one.
hint2: A tiny one inside a phone charger helps turn 220 V into 5 V.
hint3: Power stations use one to raise 25 000 V to 400 000 V.
hint4: Two windings on an iron core, with more turns on one side.

hint1: You find one inside motors and loudspeakers.
hint2: A sleeping snake can lie in this shape.
hint3: Push a magnet into it and a small current flows.
hint4: Copper going round and round many times, like a spring.

hint1: Hospitals keep one ready in case the power goes off.
hint2: China's Three Gorges Dam has more than 30 giant ones.
hint3: A bicycle dynamo is a tiny one.
hint4: Like a motor in reverse: motion goes in, voltage comes out.

hint1: Doorbells and some door locks use one.
hint2: A scrapyard crane uses one to lift old cars.
hint3: Its pull disappears when you turn the power off.
hint4: Wind wire round a nail, add a battery, and you've made one.

hint1: It is tiny, but nearly all the mass is there.
hint2: It has a positive charge.
hint3: Neutrons are packed tightly inside it.
hint4: Electrons go round it, like planets round the Sun.

hint1: A carbon atom has six of them.
hint2: Hydrogen's centre is just one of these on its own.
hint3: Count them to know which element an atom is.
hint4: Its charge is +1; an electron's is -1.

hint1: Carbon-14 has two more of these than carbon-12.
hint2: Its mass is about the same as a proton's.
hint3: It sits in the centre of an atom, next to protons.
hint4: Protons are +, electrons are -, and this one is neither.

hint1: Its symbol is Z.
hint2: In nuclide notation, it is the lower of the two values.
hint3: It is 6 for carbon, 8 for oxygen and 92 for uranium.
hint4: It counts only the positive particles in the centre of an atom.

hint1: Its symbol is A.
hint2: In nuclide notation, it is the upper of the two values.
hint3: Uranium-238 gets its name from this value.
hint4: Count every particle in the centre of an atom to get it.

hint1: Doctors use radioactive ones to see inside the body.
hint2: They act alike in chemical reactions, but their masses differ.
hint3: Atoms of one kind, with different numbers of uncharged particles.
hint4: Carbon-12 and carbon-14 are two of these.

hint1: Yellow and black warning signs are used for things like this.
hint2: Radon gas from rocks is like this.
hint3: Its atoms break down and give out tiny particles or rays.
hint4: Marie Curie's notebooks are still like this today.

hint1: A Geiger counter still clicks slowly with no source nearby.
hint2: Radon gas from the ground adds a lot of it.
hint3: Students subtract it from their readings before finding a half-life.
hint4: Low-level rays around us all the time, from space and the ground.

hint1: Smoke alarms contain a tiny source that gives these out.
